t: Browser-Based Local Code Scanner | Detect Secrets, SQL Injection, and XSS

Scan uploaded code without sending it to any server. Detect secrets, dangerous functions, SQL injection, and XSS, with severity classification, deduplication, saving and exporting results, and fix suggestions.

Yes. You can scan code inside your browser only, without sending it to any server, because this tool runs entirely locally using static pattern checks that look for secrets embedded in code, dangerous functions, SQL injection, and script injection in pages. It then classifies each result according to the severity criteria you choose, removes duplicate results, and suggests practical fixes for each issue before it becomes an actually exploitable vulnerability. No file or text leaves your device during scanning, saving, or exporting; results are stored only in your browser's local storage, and you can download them in structured formats to review later, share with your team, or attach to security review reports. You can also generate a security policy draft and a threat model ready for download and editing according to your project's nature, assets, and various deployment environments.

Are the code or results uploaded to an external server during the scan?

No. The tool runs entirely in the browser. Files are read locally, scans are saved only in your device's local storage, and files are downloaded directly from your browser without any network transmission.
What types of issues does the scan detect?

The scan detects embedded secrets such as passwords and access keys, dangerous functions such as dynamic execution and system commands, SQL injection patterns built by concatenating strings, and XSS patterns such as writing directly to HTML.
How do I control severity levels and remove duplicates?

Choose a severity for each category from the drop-down menus, set the minimum severity to show, and enable the remove duplicate results option to hide matching results with the same line, rule, and snippet.
How do I save a scan and export the results?
Select Save current scan locally, then load it later from the list. To export results, choose JSON, CSV, or SARIF; you'll get files ready for review or for other static analysis tools.
What do the Generate SECURITY.md and Generate threat model buttons do?
They generate a draft security disclosure policy and a threat model based on the current scan summary. You can review and edit the text and download it as Markdown for use in your project.

Remove the secret from the code, move it to secret environment variables, rotate it immediately if it is real, and check the Git history.
Revoke this key, issue a new key through the secrets manager, and never embed access keys in the interface.
Remove the private key from the code and repository, use a secure key store, and rotate the associated keys immediately.
Avoid dynamic execution and replace it with explicit logic or a safe parser, because the executed content may come from attacker input.
Do not pass user input to system commands; use dedicated APIs, fixed argument lists, and strict validation.
Pass a function instead of a string to the timer, because strings are executed as code and may hide malicious behavior.
Building a query with string concatenation
Use prepared statements with bound parameters, and never concatenate user input into the query string.
Passing a string directly to query execution
Use prepared statements and an allowlist for columns and tables, and apply the principle of least privilege to the database.
Use textContent or a trusted sanitization library, and never insert user data into HTML without sanitization.
Avoid document.write, and build the UI with safe DOM nodes such as createElement and textContent.
Replace HTML injection with safe node building or sanitize content before insertion.
Using a URL or hash without validation
Validate and sanitize values coming from the URL before displaying them, and avoid inserting them directly into the page.
